Is Salesforce Still The Business You Bought?

If you hold Salesforce (CRM), you likely bought into a subscription software provider known for steady growth and reliable cash generation. During its fiscal Q2 2027 earnings call in August, management noted that a $25 billion accelerated share repurchase was still under way. Has a buyback of that size changed the company behind your shares?

Partly: Salesforce's Balance Sheet Has Changed

While the core software operation looks much as it did a year ago, the underlying balance sheet looks starkly different. Debt accounted for 38.1% of the company's assets during fiscal Q2 2027, the latest reported quarter. For the fourteen years prior to the past year, that metric typically sat around 14.8%. In absolute terms, Salesforce held total debt of $41.7 billion at the end of the quarter. That compares with just $11.4 billion in cash and short-term investments.

Why Is Salesforce's Debt So High?

Salesforce is currently spending more on its own stock than its operations generate. The company deployed $35.1 billion for buybacks over the last twelve months, yet its free cash flow over the same period came in at $15.2 billion. Bridging that shortfall required Salesforce to rely on existing cash reserves or tap debt markets. During the August call, management said it expects to buy back at least 14% of the shares outstanding through the accelerated program.

The underlying business still resembles the enterprise of a year ago. Salesforce recorded an operating margin of 22% over the last twelve months, climbing slightly from 21% a year earlier. Management noted that customer attrition sits near its lowest level ever. Meanwhile, fiscal Q2 2027 revenue grew 11% from a year earlier in constant currency.

What Do You Get For Salesforce's Debt?

Shareholders walk away with a larger slice of the business. Salesforce reported 821 million diluted shares in the latest reported quarter, a drop from 962 million a year earlier. Each remaining share now holds a claim on a larger portion of the profit. The company has also acquired this stock at a discount to current trading levels. Management noted in August that shares purchased so far under the accelerated program cost an average of $176 each, below the $229.13 price where the stock now trades.

The tradeoff comes in the form of the debt Salesforce now carries. After subtracting cash, Salesforce carries debt equal to about 1.8 times a year of its earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization. The company must service interest on those obligations before any cash can reach shareholders.

One $180 Billion Family Now Controls Every Voting Share of the Company That Owns CNN, CBS, and HBO. It Only Cost About 9% of Their Fortune.
Caleb Naysmith

NY Stock Exchange by Aditya Vyas via Unsplash

David Ellison and his family invested about $17 billion to complete the takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery, according to Bloomberg's reading of public filings, which count an estimated 1.4 billion shares bought in the stock offering at $12 per share. Forbes estimated Larry Ellison's fortune at $180.9 billion as of Oct. 8, eighth in the world, making the family's check a little over 9% of the Oracle (ORCL) co-founder's paper net worth on the day the two numbers were published.

What the money bought closed on Oct. 6. The combined company is called Skydance (SKYD), and it now trades on the New York Stock Exchange as SKYD; Barchart has already covered how to approach the stock now that the merger has closed. The assets named in closing coverage include Paramount, Warner Bros., HBO and HBO Max, Paramount+, CBS, CNN, Nickelodeon, Cartoon Network, MTV, Food Network, HGTV, and Comedy Central. Warner Bros. Discovery shareholders received about $31.02 per share in cash, and Bloomberg puts the acquisition's value at $110 billion.

The prospectus supplement the company filed with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) outlines the control structure. "All matters submitted to our stockholders are decided solely by the vote of holders of our Class A Common Stock," the document says, while the Class B shares that public investors own carry no vote except where the law requires one. Harbor Lights Entertainment — the company formerly known as National Amusements — holds all of the Class A stock, and the filing states that "entities controlled by the Ellison family hold approximately 77.5% of our Class A Common Stock indirectly." Summarizing Bloomberg, Quartz puts it more simply: The Ellison family holds the largest equity stake in the combined company and, together with RedBird, controls 100% of the voting shares.

The $17 billion is not the whole equity check. The acquisition included a $47 billion equity component raised at the same $12-per-share price, so the family's equity stake is a little over a third of it. The balance came from the other investors named in the closing coverage; RedBird, which co-led the equity, and the Public Investment Fund (PIF), L'IMAD, and the Qatar Investment Authority (QIA) — three sovereign wealth funds whose individual amounts the filing Barchart read does not break out. Earlier in the bidding, while Netflix (NFLX) was still pursuing Warner Bros., Larry Ellison reportedly pledged about $40 billion personally to back the offer; Barchart covered the outcome in April as a battle Netflix lost. The gap between $40 billion pledged and about $17 billion invested is, on the filings, the sovereign-fund and RedBird money. Nothing in the record suggests the pledge was withdrawn rather than shared out.

title: Management Raised the Bar For Salesforce Stock; Does The Chart Agree?

Management Raised the Bar For Salesforce Stock; Does The Chart Agree?

Image from Pixabay

Salesforce (CRM) stock has gained 10.9% since the day before the company raised its fiscal 2027 profit forecast on August 26, 2026, outpacing a 1.1% return for the S&P 500. Yet a raised forecast is merely a projection of future performance. Investors must ask if the market is still buying into that promise today. Is that gain still building, or did it all come in the first two days?

Has Salesforce Stock Kept Climbing Since The Raise?

The short answer is not quite. While the stock initially surged, it recorded more than its entire advance in the first two days and has slipped ever since. Salesforce stock rose 22.5% over the two sessions around the release, while the S&P 500 gained just 0.7%. Investors priced in the entire release at once, absorbing both the quarter's results and the new forecast immediately. Since then the stock has fallen 9.5%, while the index has added 0.4%.

The broader trend remains upward, however. Salesforce trades 1.8% above its 50-day average, which represents the average closing price over the last 50 trading days. It also sits 14.4% above its 200-day average. When a stock price stays above both benchmarks, with the shorter average tracking higher, the chart signals a clear uptrend. Even so, Salesforce is now holding only just above its 50-day average.

What Salesforce Management Raised

Management raised its fiscal 2027 guide for earnings per share to $10.21 to $10.25, from an earlier midpoint of $7.96. Most of that guidance increase is already accounted for: second-quarter GAAP earnings per share surged to $4.29 against a $1.75 guide, boosted by discrete non-operating gains while operating income remained essentially flat with the first quarter. It is important to note this is a revised forecast for the same year, rather than a final result. The sales forecast shifted far less. Salesforce now expects fiscal 2027 revenue of $46.1 billion to $46.4 billion, sitting just 0.4% above its prior guide at the midpoint.

The company noted it raised the revenue forecast by about $300 million before currency effects. Two acquisitions, Contentful and Fin, provide $200 million of that expected contribution. The existing business performed better than planned to make up the rest. However, executives said the new forecast also includes a $100 million hit from currency moves compared with the earlier projection, which is why the final midpoint rose by a smaller margin. Management credited Slack and Agentforce, its software for AI agents, for the revenue growth in the quarter. The company guided no line lower, and the forecast for cash flow growth stayed at 4% to 5%.

title: Oracle (ORCL) Has $664B Lined Up. The Market Wants Cash First
detail:
Oracle (ORCL) Has $664B Lined Up. The Market Wants Cash First
Maham Fatima
Mon, October 12, 2026 at 7:27 AM PDT 5 min read
ORCL
Trade Oracle on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) is sitting on a pile of signed business most companies can only dream about: $664 billion in remaining performance obligations (contracted revenue not yet recognized) at the end of fiscal Q1 2027. Yet the market keeps treating the stock like a question mark, attracting retail attention similar to the favorites found on our rundown of 10 Cheap Stocks That Will Go to the Moon According to Reddit as shares recently slid alongside other AI names after a report on OpenAI's revenue, according to CNBC.

For decades, Oracle made its money selling database software and the business applications that run on top of it, from finance to HR. Today, the growth engine is Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI), which rents out computing power, much of it to companies training and running AI models.

The real question is which matters more: the backlog, or the bill for delivering it. The answer hinges on one line of the cash flow statement that's currently in the red.

The Database Toll Booth

Oracle's edge starts with switching costs. Its databases sit underneath banking systems, airline reservations, and government records, and ripping one out is slow, risky, and expensive. That installed base gives Oracle a natural audience for its cloud pitch.

The applications side shows the steadier half of the business. Cloud applications revenue reached $4.2 billion in fiscal Q1 2027, up 10%. That's not flashy, but it's recurring software revenue that tends to stay put once it's in place, securing Oracle's standing among the 10 Best Cloud Computing Stocks to Buy According to Billionaires.

Demand Is Outrunning Supply

Infrastructure is where the story shifts gears. OCI revenue hit $7.4 billion in fiscal Q1 2027, up 121%, while total cloud revenue climbed 62% to $11.6 billion. Total revenue rose 30% to $19.3 billion.

The backlog explains why management keeps leaning in. RPO grew by $209 billion year over year, and Oracle booked more than $30 billion in new AI cloud contracts during the quarter. The company says demand for AI training and inferencing is running ahead of the capacity it can supply, even after delivering more than 300,000 GPUs to AI cloud customers since the end of fiscal Q4.

Guidance points the same way. Oracle expects fiscal Q2 cloud revenue growth of 65% to 71% in dollars, and full-year revenue of at least $90 billion. On the infrastructure side, the moat looks like it's widening, though it's a race specialist AI cloud providers like CoreWeave are running too.

Can Oracle Afford Its Own Success?
